clinicalPearls: A defect, either a stress fracture or a fibrous non-union, of the pars interarticularis, most often at L5
A common cause of low back pain in adolescent athletes engaged in repetitive hyperextension such as gymnastics, cricket fast bowling, dancing, and diving
Pain is typically activity-related axial low back pain that is worsened by lumbar extension
The single-leg hyperextension (stork) test may reproduce pain on the affected side
On oblique radiographs the defect appears as a collar or broken neck on the outline of the Scotty dog
A bilateral defect may allow the vertebral body to slip forward on the one below (isthmic spondylolisthesis)
SPECT or SPECT/CT and MRI detect early, radiographically occult stress reactions and help assess fracture activity and healing potential
Most respond to activity restriction, physiotherapy, and sometimes bracing; surgical repair or fusion is reserved for refractory pain or a progressive slip
reference.pathophysiology: Spondylolysis is a defect of the pars interarticularis, the bony bridge linking the superior and inferior articular processes of a vertebra. It usually represents a fatigue (stress) fracture from repetitive hyperextension and rotational loading rather than an acute injury, and there is a recognised genetic and dysplastic predisposition. The lowest lumbar level (L5) bears the greatest shear stress and is most often affected. When the defect is bilateral the vertebral body can slip forward on the one below, producing isthmic spondylolisthesis, which may in turn narrow the foramen and place the exiting nerve root under tension.
additionalDifferentials: Vertebral osteomyelitis or tumour when red flags are present
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs including oblique views (Scotty-dog sign) and lateral views to assess any slip
MRI as the first-line advanced imaging in young patients to detect a stress reaction and avoid radiation
SPECT or SPECT/CT to assess the metabolic activity and healing potential of the defect
CT to define the bony anatomy and characterise chronicity of the defect
Standing flexion-extension radiographs to assess dynamic instability when a slip is present
redFlags: Neurological deficit or radicular symptoms suggesting nerve-root compression from a high-grade slip
Rapidly progressive slip on serial imaging
Constitutional symptoms or night pain suggesting infection or tumour
reference.prognosis: Many young patients achieve pain-free return to activity with conservative management, and early stress reactions may heal with rest; high-grade or progressive slips and persistent pain may require surgical stabilisation, but outcomes are generally good.
pitfalls: Relying on plain radiographs alone, which miss early stress reactions
Failing to monitor for slip progression during adolescent growth
Attributing all adolescent back pain to spondylolysis without excluding other causes
management: Activity modification and relative rest from the provocative hyperextension loading as first-line management
Physiotherapy with core and lumbar stabilisation once acute pain settles, with analgesia for symptom control
Bracing with an antilordotic orthosis to promote healing of an active pars stress reaction in adolescents
Graded, supervised return to sport once pain-free, with monitoring of healing on imaging
Surgical repair or segmental fusion reserved for persistent pain despite prolonged conservative care or progression to symptomatic isthmic spondylolisthesis
Surveillance for slip development with standing lateral and flexion-extension radiographs when the defect is bilateral
